content: Chlorproguanil-dapsone has been evaluated as a potential alternative treatment for uncomplicated falciparum malaria, particularly in regions of Africa where resistance to chloroquine and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is prevalent. The objective of this review was to compare the efficacy and safety of chlorproguanil-dapsone with other antimalarial drugs. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and Biosis Previews, up to May 2004. Conference proceedings and reference lists were also reviewed, and researchers in the field were contacted. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing chlorproguanil-dapsone to other antimalarial treatments. Six trials, involving a total of 3,352 participants, met the inclusion criteria. In one trial, a single dose of chlorproguanil-dapsone (1.2 mg chlorproguanil) resulted in fewer treatment failures compared to chloroquine. However, in three trials, chlorproguanil-dapsone was associated with more treatment failures and a higher prevalence of parasitaemia at day 28 compared to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. Two trials evaluated a three-dose regimen of chlorproguanil-dapsone (2 mg chlorproguanil) in newly diagnosed patients. By day 7, treatment failures were significantly lower with chlorproguanil-dapsone compared to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (Risk Ratio [RR] 0.30, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.19 to 0.49; n = 827, 1 trial). Similarly, by day 14, fewer treatment failures were observed with chlorproguanil-dapsone (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.53; n = 1,709, 1 trial). However, neither trial reported total treatment failures by day 28. Another trial specifically included participants who had previously failed treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. Across the trials, adverse event reporting was inconsistent. However, chlorproguanil-dapsone was associated with a higher incidence of adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation compared to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (RR 4.54, 95% CI 1.74 to 11.82; n = 829, 1 trial). Additionally, chlorproguanil-dapsone was linked to a greater risk of red blood cell disorders (RR 2.86, 95% CI 1.33 to 6.13; n = 1,850, 1 trial). The authors concluded that there is insufficient data to fully assess the effects of the current standard three-dose chlorproguanil-dapsone regimen (2 mg chlorproguanil). They emphasized the need for randomized controlled trials with follow-up to day 28, comprehensive adverse event reporting, and intention-to-treat analyses to guide policy decisions. However, as of 2008, the review is no longer being updated because chlorproguanil-dapsone has been withdrawn from use.
